newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain plugs tax loophole on share buybacks.

text.p: The British government plugged a tax loophole on Tuesday which has allowed a growing band of companies to enrich investors through share buyback schemes in a move which will save Britain up to 400 million pounds a year.

British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said shareholders who previously would have been able to claim tax credits on share buyacks or special dividend payouts will no longer be able to do so as of October 8.
He said in a statement that the move stemmed from "...the growing loss of tax through schemes involving companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends."

The decision will hit British companies who so far this year have announced plans to spend up to 2.5 billion pounds ($4 billion) in buying back their own shares, with this total seen rising to four billion pounds by the end of the year.
Share buybacks are most beneficial to tax-exempt shareholders, principally pension funds, who can claim tax credits from the government.

"We have seen recently companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends in such a way that the proceeds end up almost entirely in the hands of those who are entitled to payment of a tax credit," Clarke said.
"This has costs for the Exchequer, and if action is not taken soon that cost would escalate," he said.

He said a provision would be included in the next Finance Bill to change the tax treatment of such schemes and added that this would result in cost savings of as much as 400 million pounds a year from 1998-99.

"The government takes a firm attitude on tax avoidance...the scale of the exploitation means it had reached a point where the Chancellor had to act because of the costs involved," said a spokeswoman for the British tax authorities.
Shares in a string of top British companies planning buybacks fell amid concerns that the ruling makes these schemes less attractive to their major investors.

Shares in international news and information organisation Reuters Holdings Plc, which announced plans for a 613 million pounds bonus share issue in September, were 19-1/2p lower at 757-1/2p by midday on Tuesday.

Reuters was due to hold a special shareholders' meeting on Wednesday to approve this scheme and a source close to Treasury ministers said that they were "...well aware of this date" when deciding on the timing of Tuesday's announcement.
"A decision after that date would clearly have been more difficult for the company," the source told Reuters.
Other companies similarly affected included several banks and utilities who have also announced either buybacks or special dividends.
Banking group Barclays Plc was down 19-1/2p at 757-1/2p and National Westminister Bank was off 11p at 701.
Water company Severn Trent slipped 5-12p to 600-1/2p and energy firm PowerGen was off 9-1/2p at 480p.
The new ruling relates to tax credits linked to share buybacks or special dividends linked to share consolidations or to takeovers.
Companies often use special dividends as a sweetener to shareholders when launching a takeover bid for a rival firm and tax experts said the new rules would affect this.

"I am sure it will reduce the number of company buybacks. What happens right now is not fiddling the tax system...it's the way it works," said John Whiting, tax partner at Price Waterhouse. ($1=.6401 Pound)
